what_it_did.what_the_split_means: A mechanical commit republishes an unchanged net -- the report, the dashboard, the state files. Counting those as work would make a quiet day look busy, so they are separated rather than filtered: they happened, they are just not progress.

what_it_decided.thesis_read: Three hours, seven commits, three substantive, and this is the best stretch the thesis has had. The price ladder landed in full and it ANSWERED the director's question rather than deferring it. The fourth way for the arm's advantage to be hollow -- that it comes from PRICE rather than from prediction -- is refused: over six rungs the world's churn probability rises 1.16x faster than the company believes it does (median over decisions), the two slopes agree to within 16% on all three x-axes (0.86 / 0.87 / 0.86), and the bias runs toward the world biting HARDER, which is the opposite of the forgiving-curve story. It earned that on a design that fixes the thing the realised A/B could not: rung zero reproduces the flat-rules control to the last decimal (net margin GBP 16,354.767758 on both sides, roster difference none), the rung is scored INSIDE `decide_margin` so the belief describes the price actually offered, and the scored price is reconciled against the world's own logged `price_differential_vs_svt` at 58 renewals with a largest gap of 0.005 percentage points. The paired design turns 6 decisions into 36 observations, so "effective n is 4" is superseded for the slope question. That is inference being measured honestly, and it is what this project is for. It also found something bigger than what it was sent to find, and it is a LEVEL error, not a slope error: at the flat rule the company believes these customers are 32.8% likely to leave and the world realises 5.5%. A supplier that thinks its book is six times more flighty than it is prices BELOW what the world would tolerate -- money left on the table, not taken from a soft curve. That is a company-side calibration finding, it is the company's own affair under the wall, and it is now the largest single belief error this project has measured. Against that, the number that has not moved is the one nearest the thesis's centre. EP1's coupled gap is still 2.529 -- the company's per-customer CLV carries LESS information about realised lifetime margin than assigning every account the population mean, by two and a half times -- and the ledger is still stamped 2026-08-26T11:46:22Z with `distinct_hazards: 1`, `hazard_histogram {"0.05": 33}` and a believed tenure of 20.0 years for all 33 graded accounts. The thesis says there has to be a baseline to beat. `couple_clv` is that baseline, built and running, and the company loses to it. Fourth naming, fourth stretch drawn-and-unchanged. I think I now know why, and it is not the tick: every instruction so far, mine included by inheritance, said "widen the inputs", and none of them looked at where the field being read is WRITTEN. `company/analytics/customer_value_view.py:223` takes `r["churn_probability"]` from the `churn_risk` map, and that map is written at `saas/churn_model.py:116` by `build_churn_risk` -- the same module the ladder's own independence block names as a component of the WORLD's realised churn probability (observed: both call sites; inferred: that this shared provenance is why four passes did plumbing and stopped). So EP1's hazard is not a thin company belief, it is a borrowed one, and "widen it" was the wrong instruction four times running. Two smaller readings. EP13 did the first of its two acts and did it properly -- 11,940 B rehomed to 2,293 B, 348 B from wedging every lane's commit, verbatim and round-trip asserted -- and left the second undone for the third stretch; and I have to correct my predecessor on it, because the correction changes the work: L2 is "mechanically real, happy path", the coupled rung binds L3, so EP13 at 2 with no coupler is not a false level claim. It is an atom with no path to 3. Lastly, `run_value_cycle_ab` was not run for the fourth stretch running, and this time it was CLAIMED at 02:44 by a Lane 0 tick and released on the clock at 04:50 with nothing landed and no paths ever bound to the claim. Two claim-and-drops on the same six-line mechanical instruction is R3 territory, so it is first here with an escape hatch written into it rather than a third identical restatement. And the brief handed me `steered: true` again: the two ids it credits are EP1, which did not move, and EP13, which moved halfway, while the item that landed in full was a Lane 0 slug the control cannot represent. I read the commits.

focus.what: Two commands, in this order, landing after EACH one rather than batching. FIRST `python3 -m tools.run_value_cycle_ab` with no `--end-year`, then edit the headline table in `docs/design/THE_VALUE_CYCLE_REALISED_AB.md` so the current row names the book it ran on -- account count, segment split, git commit -- keeping every superseded row with its supersession note, and quote `gross_to_net_bridge`, `bound_attribution` and `cross_section_reconciliation` including `unexplained_residual_gbp`. SECOND `python3 -m tools.run_price_ladder` with no `--end-year`, which is the increment the ladder's own section names as immediate, and re-read that section's two headline claims against the wider common set. The full-window ladder is seven `run_phase4c` passes; if that is too long for one tick, drop to `--rungs 0,0.5,1,2` at FULL window rather than six rungs at 2019 -- keep rung zero, it is the null control the whole reading rests on. Bind the paths of each landing with `delivery_lane.record_landing` as it lands. IF EITHER TOOL ERRORS OR REFUSES, that is the deliverable: record the error verbatim as a finding, land the other one, and do not let a broken tool cost the whole item. R14: every figure carries its clock.
focus.why: The A/B has been named first twice, claimed twice by a Lane 0 tick, and dropped twice with no paths bound to either claim, so the stall was invisible until a clock timeout -- the repair is an escape hatch and a landing record, not a third restatement of the same six lines. The ladder half is different: its own artefact says the common population is 6 where a full window should reach 15-20, and that "six decisions is six decisions" is the weakest thing about the only result that has actually answered the director. Both go FIRST because focus item two changes the belief these instruments measure; run after that change and the numbers describe a company that no longer exists, which is exactly the defect the 26 August book already caused once. Finished when the newest `value_cycle_ab*.json` carries all three instrument keys with live figures, the newest ladder artefact reports `report_end: null`, and the artefact's current rows name their own books. Whatever the residual and whatever the slope ratio, publishing it is the deliverable -- a bridge that does not close is a finding, not an embarrassment.

focus.what: Fifth naming and a DIFFERENT instruction, because the previous four were wrong. Do not widen the inputs to the hazard. Change WHOSE hazard it is. `company/analytics/clv_three_horizon.py` takes `hazard = latest.churn_probability` and the term `1.0 / hazard`; that field arrives via `company/analytics/customer_value_view.py:223` from `churn_risk`, which is written at `saas/churn_model.py:116` by `build_churn_risk` -- a module the price ladder's own `world_curve_vs_belief.independence` block names as a component of the WORLD's realised churn probability. Verify that chain first and say what you find; if it holds, the company's valuation is resting its lifetime term on a borrowed number, and the fix is to have EP1 form its own per-account estimate through `company/crm/churn_model.py::estimate_churn_probability`, which the pricing arm already uses and which already takes the right signature. Two things travel with it. The level: that estimator believes 0.328 at the flat rule where the world realised 0.055, so applying it raw would trade a level-right constant for a dispersed 6x-hot one -- calibrate the level AT EP1'S POINT OF USE against the company's OWN observed renewal outcomes (the ledger's `hazard_calibration` already publishes 0.05 believed against 0.0532 realised over 263 decisions, which is the company's own history and is on the legal side of the wall), and leave `company/crm/churn_model.py` itself untouched this stretch so the pricing arm does not move under item one's feet. And the wall: name every new input with the observable it comes from and clear it through `company/interfaces/sim_interface.py`, the only door. Then re-measure with `python3 -m tools.couple_clv`.
focus.why: "Decisions customer-by-customer on lifetime value" and a lifetime term of 20.0 years for all 33 graded accounts are the same claim and its refutation. The gap is 2.529 against a no-skill predictor that assigns everyone the population mean -- the thesis says there must be a baseline to beat, this coupler IS that baseline, and the company loses to it by two and a half times. That is the single worst reading in the project and it sits at the thesis's centre. It is second only because item one must read the current belief before item two changes it. Finished when the graded population shows more than one distinct hazard, the wall clearance for each new input is written down, and the ledger's next entry comes from a changed estimator rather than a changed sample. R12: report the gap whichever way it moves, and do not tune anything toward a smaller one -- a worse gap from an honest per-account hazard is a publishable result and a better gap from a fitted one is not. If the coupled rung is genuinely met, a move to 3 is available on that evidence -- self-certify with `record_level_up_self_certified`, never `--no-verify` a `level_current` change. If it does not move a fifth time, the atom is not the problem and the next act is to decompose it, not to name it a sixth.

what_next.why_this_is_here: Direction multiplies the draw's existing weights and can never zero one, so it can only ever be ignored -- never obeyed by force. Whether it was actually followed is therefore a measurement, not an assumption.

how_to_read_this: The delivery seat wakes on a timer, reads the last stretch, and writes direction -- never code. What it decides biases which work the ticks draw and can never block any of it. Everything on this page is read from a committed record; nothing here is computed a second time.
